title: Emerging Technologies Classification and Adoption Strategies (Module 8 deck)
author: Andres Fortino (course deck, user-supplied)
type: course analytical framework
locator: Slides 26-35 technology classification; 37-47 adoption rules; 48-49 Osborne case; 54 Module 9 preview (proof of concept, task-technology fit); 61 classification changes with application
supports: Four classes. Bleeding edge: extremely new (about 6 months to 2 years), expensive, high risk from instability, complex and not well understood. Leading edge: stable but new (2-5 years), has crossed the chasm, adopted by the early majority, and a major part of the industry uses it. Commodity: routine cost of business, lowest cost matters. Trailing edge: older than 5 years. Adoption rules: #1 wait for the technology to cross the chasm before adopting; #2 use pilot projects to test untested or underdeveloped technologies; #3 adopt a technology that has crossed as soon as possible; #4 periodically replace what is too old; #5 research whether it has crossed; #6 switch messaging to reach the tipping point; #7 know the adoption style your job requires; #8 keep a balanced portfolio. Summary: wait until crossed, invest in leading edge, pilot bleeding edge, dispose of trailing edge. The same technology can be bleeding edge generally and leading edge in a particular application.
does_not_support: Thresholds for a specific case; the ages (6 months to 2 years; 2-5 years) are rules of thumb.

title: The Diffusion of Emerging Technologies (Module 6 deck)
author: Andres Fortino (course deck, user-supplied)
type: course analytical framework
supports: Adopt early only if the pay-off is high in a short time and you are willing to abandon it; otherwise track adoption and adopt after the technology has crossed.
does_not_support: Case-specific conclusions.

title: Assignments 3-5 specialist outputs (Innovation and Disruption; Promethean; Diffusion)
author: Minghan Liu
type: upstream team-agent outputs
supports: A3: the SPS proposal is a proposed incremental, sustaining process innovation; compare staff-only, simple retrieval and the proposed agent before any pilot. A4: agentic AI is a Breakthrough with an UNRESOLVED Potential-Promethean candidacy; broad significance carries Low weight; any adoption step must pass the incremental-counterfactual test. A5: generative AI among people and FAQ chatbots in admissions are past take-off; agentic AI in organizations is before the chasm; tool-using recruitment agents are at innovators/early adopters; observability is the binding factor; fast-follower timing is 'prepare and trial now'.
does_not_support: Independent evidence; prior AI-assisted student analyses used as inputs.

title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
author: Thomas Kwa et al. (METR)
type: independent capability evaluation (reused from A4 register)
supports: Frontier 50%-task-completion time horizon about 50 minutes (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, early 2025); horizons have doubled roughly every seven months since 2019 and may have accelerated in 2024.
does_not_support: Real-world reliability outside the software task suite; the five-year extrapolation is a projection with stated external-validity limits.

title: The 2026 AI Index Report
author: Stanford HAI
type: independent annual indicator compilation (reused from A4 register)
supports: OSWorld agent accuracy rose from about 5% (2024) to 66.3% (2025), still below a 72.35% human baseline; generative AI reached 53% adoption within three years, faster than the internet or computers at the same stage; US AI investment $285.88 billion in 2025; a record 362 reported AI incidents in 2025.
does_not_support: Field reliability in consequential workflows; investment and adoption speed are not evidence of barrier dissolution (C2).

title: Generative AI at Work
author: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
date: NBER WP 31161 (2023); Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2):889-942 (2025)
type: field study (staggered rollout) (reused from A4 register)
supports: An AI conversational assistant raised customer-support productivity 14% on average (issues resolved per hour) across 5,179 agents, 34% for novice and low-skilled workers, minimal for the most experienced: a measured gain and a skill-compression (democratizing) mechanism in a support setting analogous to applicant inquiries.
does_not_support: Autonomous agent performance (the tool assisted humans); higher-education transfer; barrier dissolution.

title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
author: Frank F. Xu et al. (CMU and others)
type: independent agent benchmark (reused from A4 register)
supports: The most competitive agent completed 30% of simulated workplace tasks autonomously; more difficult long-horizon tasks remain beyond current systems.
does_not_support: Current frontier performance after the tested models; production reliability.

title: Building effective agents
author: Anthropic
type: vendor engineering guidance (reused from A4 register)
locator: What are agents; When to use agents
supports: Workflows orchestrate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; agents dynamically direct their own processes and tool use; agents trade latency and cost for performance and carry compounding-error risk; start with the simplest solution.
does_not_support: Independent evidence of agent superiority or reliability.

title: Large Firms With at Least 20 Employees Biggest AI Users
author: U.S. Census Bureau (Grundy, Breaux, Khatiwoda)
type: nationally representative business survey (reused from A5 register)
locator: Business Trends and Outlook Survey AI supplement
supports: 19.8% of U.S. businesses reported using AI in any business function in the last two weeks; 17-20% from December 2025 to May 2026; 37% of firms with 250+ employees; Information sector 39.7%. Question broadened in November 2025 from 'producing goods or services' to 'any business function'.
does_not_support: Agents specifically; educational services not reported. Earlier BTOS figures are not directly comparable.

title: Gartner Hype Cycle Identifies Top AI Innovations in 2025
author: Gartner (via Business Wire)
type: analyst positioning (reused from A5 register)
supports: AI agents placed at the Peak of Inflated Expectations on the 2025 Hype Cycle for AI.
does_not_support: Measured adoption. A hype position describes attention and expectations, not diffusion.

title: Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027
author: Gartner
type: analyst forecast and non-random poll (reused from A5 register)
supports: January 2025 poll of 3,412 webinar attendees: 19% significant agentic AI investment, 42% conservative, 31% wait-and-see; over 40% of agentic projects forecast to be cancelled by end-2027; only about 130 of thousands of 'agentic AI' vendors judged real ('agent washing').
does_not_support: Measured adoption; the poll is self-selected.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education (Ellucian 2026 AI report)
author: Ellucian
type: vendor survey (779 administrators, 300+ institutions, 93% U.S.) (reused from A5 register)
supports: Institutional AI use 66% (49% in 2024); 36% of Marketing, Admissions and Enrollment respondents use chatbots for FAQs; data security/privacy is the top institutional barrier (56%); 14% of executive respondents report a dedicated AI budget. No share for AI agents is reported.
does_not_support: Representativeness (vendor customers and contacts); agentic use.

title: Survey: Higher Ed AI Adoption Faces Financial, Policy Hurdles (EDUCAUSE 2025 AI Landscape Study)
author: GovTech reporting EDUCAUSE
type: secondary report of an association survey (reused from A5 register)
supports: 57% say AI is a strategic priority; 39% have AI acceptable-use policies; only 9% say privacy/security policies adequately address AI; only 2% fund AI with new sources; a 'widening digital divide' with larger institutions ahead.
does_not_support: Admissions-specific or agent-specific adoption; secondary report.

title: Unity Environmental University taps Agentforce and Education Cloud
author: Salesforce
type: vendor customer story (reused from A5 register)
supports: A university planned to deploy recruitment agents on its website to answer prospective-student questions, handle requests for information and guide applications, with hand-off to staff; it expected to save $800 of staff time per web RFI.
does_not_support: Measured results; the deployment was planned at publication and the savings are a projection.

title: Agentforce for Education: Recruitment and Admissions pre-built skill; Dreamforce 2025 education keynote summary
author: Salesforce; Cloud for Good (partner)
type: vendor product page and partner summary (reused from A5 register)
supports: A pre-built recruitment/admissions agent skill exists (answer questions from knowledge articles, create information requests, register campus tours, start applications); partner summary lists recruitment and RFI skills as generally available with some items in beta. This is change-agent activity that raises trialability.
does_not_support: Customer counts or outcomes; the product page itself warns features 'may not be currently available'.

title: Meet the NYUAdmissionsBot
author: NYU Admissions
type: organization primary source (reused from A5 register)
supports: NYU Admissions offers a generative AI admissions bot on its admissions site and applicant portal, available 24/7; it hands off to a live agent or a contact form when it cannot answer.
does_not_support: SPS graduate admissions specifically; agentic actions; vendor; usage.

title: NYU SPS Graduate Admissions
author: NYU School of Professional Studies
type: organization primary source (reused from A5 register)
supports: Phone/email contact, weekday appointments, information sessions and 'For immediate assistance, try our chatbot, Violet.'
does_not_support: Violet's architecture, tool use, vendor or usage.

title: BC Tribunal Confirms Companies Remain Liable for Information Provided by AI Chatbot (Moffatt v. Air Canada)
author: American Bar Association, Business Law Today
type: secondary report of a tribunal decision
supports: British Columbia's Civil Resolution Tribunal held Air Canada liable for negligent misrepresentation after its website chatbot gave wrong bereavement-fare information. It rejected the argument that the chatbot was 'a separate legal entity'; the company 'still bore responsibility for all the information on its website, whether it came from a static page or a chatbot.' Damages were about CAD 650.
does_not_support: U.S. law or higher-education liability; a small-claims tribunal, not a court precedent. Used only to show that an organization owns what its conversational agent tells people.

title: Salesforce Introduces New Flexible Agentforce Pricing
author: Salesforce
type: vendor pricing announcement
supports: Flex Credits: an agent action consumes 20 credits ($0.10 per action); packs of 100,000 credits cost $500; earlier conversational pricing was $2 per conversation; per-user licences were announced for later availability.
does_not_support: Total cost of ownership (integration, review, monitoring, correction) or current negotiated prices; one vendor only.

title: The AI Act implementation timeline: What changes under the AI Omnibus?
author: Future of Privacy Forum
type: secondary legal analysis
supports: The AI Omnibus (published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026) moves Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 instead of 2 August 2026; Article 50 transparency obligations became generally applicable on 2 August 2026.
does_not_support: Whether a particular SPS use is in scope; any U.S. law. Legal determinations belong to compliance.

title: AI Act Service Desk: Education and vocational training (Annex III point 3)
author: European Commission AI Act Service Desk
type: official regulatory guidance page
supports: High-risk education uses include AI systems intended to determine access or admission, or to assign persons to education institutions (3a), to evaluate learning outcomes (3b), to assess the appropriate level of education (3c), and to monitor prohibited student behaviour (3d).
does_not_support: Whether an applicant-support agent that excludes admission decisions is in scope; that depends on design and intended purpose and requires legal review.

title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
author: NIST
type: public risk framework
supports: Generated misinformation (confabulation) and human-AI configuration are named risk categories requiring explicit controls such as human oversight.
does_not_support: Legal clearance; a guaranteed safe deployment.
